Anna hummingbirds (Calypte anna) exhibit a fascinating life history shaped by their high metabolic demands and seasonal breeding ecology. Field studies tracking marked individuals have documented that eggs are incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], with hatching occurring after an average of 20.2 days [ab = 20.2 days], a period consistent with the 18 to 23 day range reported in avifaunal databases. At emergence, the tiny altricial nestlings weigh a mere 0.56 grams [Ww0 = 0.56 grams], reflecting the substantial energetic investment required to produce viable offspring from such minute initial mass. These chicks develop rapidly within the nest, growing under the constant warmth provided by the brooding female.

As the nestling period progresses, growth proceeds at a remarkable pace fueled by the protein-rich diet of insects and nectar delivered by both parents. The young birds achieve fledging weight at approximately 3.8 grams [Wwx = approximately 3.8 grams], a threshold that marks their readiness for the energetically demanding transition to independent flight. Under the thermal conditions typical of the species' active metabolic state, maintained at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the time since birth at fledging averages 16.5 days [tx = 16.5 days], though published accounts note a broader range of 14 to 19 days depending on food availability and brood size. This brief nestling period is characteristic of small-bodied hummingbirds and allows multiple brooding attempts within a single breeding season.

Following the fledging of young, juvenile Anna hummingbirds enter a period of somatic growth and feather molt before reaching sexual maturity. The time since birth at puberty, when gonadal development is complete and reproductive competence is first achieved, occurs at 240 days [tp = 240 days] under the standard body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This relatively delayed onset of maturity compared to some small passerines likely reflects the energetic costs associated with maintaining the extremely high metabolic rate required for hovering flight. Juvenile birds must also acquire sufficient fat reserves to survive the non-breeding season before initiating their first breeding attempt the following year.

The first reproductive event in the life of a female Anna hummingbird typically occurs at an age of approximately one year. More precisely, the time since birth at first brood is 365 days [tR = 365 days] when measured at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], a timing that aligns well with the species' annual breeding cycle and the availability of floral resources in their coastal California and Pacific Northwest habitats. Females lay 1 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 3 eggs per clutch], and produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], a modest reproductive output that is typical of long-lived hummingbirds. This single annual brood strategy contrasts with the multiple broods observed in some tropical congeners.

Maximum longevity records for Anna hummingbirds, derived from banding returns and mark-recapture studies, indicate an impressive lifespan of 8.5 years [am = 8.5 years] when maintained at a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This remarkable lifespan relative to body mass is among the highest recorded for any hummingbird species and reflects a slow life history pace for such a metabolically active lineage. Adult females reach an ultimate wet weight of 4.0 grams [Wwi = 4.0 grams], while males are slightly heavier at 4.5 grams [Wwi = 4.5 grams], a sexual size dimorphism that may relate to male-male competition for mating territories. These modest adult masses belie the extraordinary physiological capacities that define this iconic western North American species.
